---
title: "CLI Commands"
---

This page documents the six `{baler}` subcommands: what each one does, when you'd reach for it, and what its flags actually change. It's written for people using `{baler}` to manage `{box}` modules, not for people working on `{baler}`'s own source.

Every subcommand exits non-zero and prints `error: ...` to stderr on failure, so you can rely on that in scripts or CI without parsing output.

## Initialization and Scaffolding

Through `baler init` command, this will set up a module project. It works in two ways, depending on whether you give it a name:

1.  When you supplied the `<name>`, it scaffolds a new module project from scratch, in a new directory.

    ``` bash
    baler init <name> [--dir-name <dir>] [--native <lang>] [--backend <backend>]
    ```
    
2.  Without one, it initializes the directory you are already in, like `uv init` or `cargo init`.

    ``` bash
    baler init [--name <name>] [--src <dir>] [--native <lang>] [--backend <backend>]
    ```

Either way, `baler.toml` is the most required file to interact with `{baler}`. And then this following table summarizes how `baler init` behaves:


| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<name>` | The module's name. Used as the default project directory name (`<name>-proj`), the default source directory name, and the `name` field written into `baler.toml`. Leave it out to initialize the current directory instead. |
| `--dir-name <dir>` | Only with `<name>`. Use a different project directory name instead of `<name>-proj`. |
| `--name <name>` | Only without `<name>`. The module's name, instead of the one worked out from the current directory (see [The current directory](#the-current-directory)). Anything goes; it isn't checked. |
| `--src <dir>` | Only without `<name>`. The directory holding the module's source, relative to the current directory. Written as `src` in `baler.toml`, unless it is the module's own name, which is the default. It must be an existing directory inside the project. |
| `--native <lang>` | Scaffold a module with compiled code instead of pure R: `c` for C, `cpp` for C++. Sets up a starter source file, build configuration, and the loader code that runs `dyn.load()` automatically. Leave this out for a plain R module. |
| `--backend <backend>` | Only relevant with `--native cpp`. Which C++ binding library to scaffold: `rcpp` (the default) or `cpp11`. |

When `--native` is not passed, this will ignore `--backend` parameter, and won't generate the files under the chosen language, just their pure R versions.

### A new project

Once executed with a `<name>`, the following files:

1.  `baler.toml`
2.  `README.md`
3.  And R source files under a folder containing the source code of the module

are generated. It only fails without changing anything if the target directory already exists, so it's safe to run and see the error rather than risk overwriting something.

Here's an example:

``` bash
baler init stats_native
```

### The current directory

Without a `<name>`, `baler init` sets up the directory you are in. It always writes `baler.toml` there. If `baler.toml` already exists, it stops with an error and writes nothing.

There are two cases of what else it does depends on the directory:

1.  When the directory is *empty* (not counting the hidden entries such as `.git`), it also adds `README.md` and an example module, in a folder named after the module. This is the same layout as a new project, only in place. `--native` and `--backend` apply here.

2.  Otherwise, when it is *not empty*, i.e. you already have the source code files and/or anything, it writes `baler.toml` and nothing else. Your files are left as they are, and no example module or README is added. `--native` is rejected here, because scaffolding native code into a project that already has files could overwrite them. Add the native code yourself instead; it is detected automatically.

#### The module's name

The module's name is the directory's name, as is. For example, when the current directory you initialized is named `weather/` will give `weather`, and `tidyverse-module/` gives `tidyverse-module`. `baler init` do not strip or check anything. That's because a name that [isn't syntactic in R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/names-values.html#non-syntactic), such as `my-module`, still works, since `box::use()` accepts it in backticks. To use a different name, pass `--name` or edit `name` in `baler.toml`. 

#### The source directory

`src` in `baler.toml` says where the module's source lives. By default it is a folder named after the module. If your module is in a different folder, pass `--src <dir>` or edit `src` in `baler.toml`.

If the source directory doesn't exist, `baler init` prints a warning and still writes `baler.toml`. Keep in mind that `baler bundle` needs an `__init__.r` in that directory, which `baler init` doesn't create for code that is already there.

#### Examples

Here are three common situations.

1.  You are in an empty directory called `weather/`. Running `baler init` gives you a module named `weather`, plus `README.md` and an example module in `weather/weather/`. The same goes for a directory called `tidyverse-module/`, where the module is named `tidyverse-module`.

2.  You are in an existing `weather/` project whose source code is in `weather-module/`:

    ``` 
    └── weather/
        ├── LICENSE.md
        └── weather-module/
            ├── __init__.r
            └── submodule/
                ├── __init__.r
                └── source.r
    ```

    The module is named `weather`, but the source isn't in a folder with that name, so point `baler init` at it:

    ``` bash
    baler init --src weather-module
    ```

    `baler.toml` is the only new file, and it records the source directory as `src = "weather-module"`.

3.  You are in `tidyverse-module/`, but you want a different module name. Pass `--name`:

    ``` bash
    baler init --name tidyverse
    ```

## Native compiled code compilation

As what the [official documentation](https://klmr.me/box/articles/compiled-code.html) of `{box}` R package said, one module can handle native compiled codes. `{baler}` gives you an alternative approach to manage module's native code (C, C++, ...) right where the source lives, for quick local iteration while developing. It never deletes the source afterward, which is what sets it apart from the compile step that happens automatically during `install`. For this one, use `baler compile` and here's the following anatomy: 

``` bash
baler compile [<path>] [--clean] [--rebuild]
```

The following table summarizes the following bracketed "parameters" above: 

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<path>` | The project's root directory. If you leave this out, it defaults to the current directory, so plain `baler compile` works from inside a project. |
| `--clean` | Deletes this module's compiled output and anything cached from previous builds, then stops without compiling anything. Use this when you just want a clean slate, not a new build. |
| `--rebuild` | Throws away anything cached from a previous build first, then compiles again for real, even if nothing in the source actually changed. Useful when you've upgraded your compiler or toolchain and want to confirm the module still builds correctly, since an unchanged build would otherwise just reuse the old result. |

A plain `baler compile`, with neither flag, only recompiles when the source has actually changed since the last build; otherwise it reuses the previous result to save time. `--clean` and `--rebuild` do opposite things and can't be used together, passing both is an error.

## Bundling and Packaging

Similar to `pkgbuild::build()` (or `devtools::build()`) and an analogue for `R CMD build`, `baler bundle` now bundles a module's source, creating into a single `.tar.gz` archive that can be installed elsewhere, shared with someone else, or attached to a GitHub release. Here's the anatomy of the `baler bundle` command: 

``` bash
# If `<path>` isn't supplied
# Then `.` argument is passed by default
baler bundle [<path>] [--locked]
```

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<path>` | The project's root directory, wherever `baler.toml` lives. Defaults to `.`. |
| `--locked` | Fail instead of warning when `baler.lock` is missing, unreadable, or doesn't match `baler.toml`. Like `cargo publish --locked`. The lock ships inside the bundle, so a stale one breaks installs of it. Without the flag, `bundle` only warns. |

::: {.callout-note title="Legacy of {carrier}" collapse="true"}
It is decided that the `--binary` or `--keep-source` are now dropped. Now, what the archive contains is decided by `[compiled-code]` in `baler.toml` through the following:

-  When `binary = true` is declared under the `[compiled-code]` from `baler.toml`, `{baler}` will compile any native code in the module first, and include the compiled artifact in the archive. Without it, only source is bundled, and compiled code has to be built again on install.

-  When `keep_source = true` is declared under the `[compiled-code]` from `baler.toml`, the native source code will be kept on the archives. This is only valid together with `binary = true`. 

The resulting archive is named `<name>_<version>.tar.gz` (`<name>` is what you set as `name` under `[project]` in `baler.toml`), and written to whatever directory you ran the command from. The execution fails if the source directory is empty, or if `baler.toml` is missing or can't be parsed. A bundle built with `binary = true` only works reliably on the exact platform and R version it was built for. There's currently no automatic check that warns you, or falls back to compiling, when installing one on a mismatched machine, even if `keep_source = true` was set at bundle time.
:::

## Module installation

As long as the `{box}` module is configured by `{baler}`, you can install that `{box}` module so that other machines and/or projects can load it with `box::use()`. This is `{baler}`'s equivalent of `install.packages()`.

``` bash
baler install <name> --repo <url> [--version <constraint>] [--install-deps [--extras]]
baler install --path <dir-or-tar.gz> [--install-deps [--extras]]
baler install --git <url> [--branch <ref> | --tag <ref> | --rev <ref>] [--module-dir <dir>] [--install-deps [--extras]]
# Always look up at tarball source only
baler install --url <tarball> [--install-deps [--extras]]
```

Use exactly one of `<name>`, `--path`, `--git`, or `--url` to say where to install from. Using more than one, or none, is an error.


| Form | What it does |
|---|---|
| `<name>` (positional) | A bare module name for a registry lookup, nothing else. Never guessed as a path, mirrors `cargo install <crate>`/`pip install <pkg>` exactly. Needs `--repo` or it errors, telling you to use `--repo`, `--path`, `--git`, or `--url` instead. |
| `--path <dir-or-tar.gz>` | A directory containing `baler.toml`, or a `.tar.gz` produced by `baler bundle`. The only way to install from a local source, mirrors `cargo install --path`. |
| `--git <url>` | A GitHub repository URL, e.g. `https://github.com/user/repo`. Fetches through GitHub's tarball API, not generic git, so a GitLab or self-hosted URL won't work despite the flag's name. Add `--branch`, `--tag`, or `--rev` to pin a ref (pick one), and `--module-dir <dir>` if the repo holds more than one module. |
| `--url <tarball>` | Installs directly from an already-bundled archive URL, such as a GitHub Release asset from `baler bundle`. Must end in `.tar.gz`, checked up front. |
| `--repo <url>` | Looks up `<name>` in a module registry at `<url>`. Registries aren't built yet, so this currently just fails with a clear "not implemented" error. Add `--version <constraint>` once registries exist. |

The extra parameter, `--install-deps`, downloads and installs the module's dependencies, whether CRAN-style R packages (they are linked from CRAN by default) or `box-bale` modules. Without it, `{baler}` still shows what it would install, but doesn't fetch anything. Installing a module that's already installed under the same name replaces the old copy.

`--extras` also installs the R packages (and `{box}` modules) the module declares under `[extras]`, such as test frameworks or development tooling. It only works together with `--install-deps`, since extras are R packages installed from CRAN, and passing it alone is an error. If the module declares nothing under `[extras]`, `{baler}` says so and installs nothing extra. When the module has a `baler.lock`, the extras are installed at the versions pinned there, transitive packages included, and a missing or outdated extras pin is an error telling you to run `baler lock`. Without a lock, `[extras]` is resolved together with the regular dependencies, and a package declared in both with different version constraints is an error. Without `--extras`, extras-only pins are never installed.

`baler install` never writes `baler.lock`. If the lock doesn't match `baler.toml`, the install fails and points you to `baler lock`. On the other hand, with no lock at all, it resolves fresh.

Installing via `--git` obviously needs internet access to reach GitHub, and those requests aren't authenticated. If you're installing several `--git` sources in a short window, for example in a CI pipeline, you would run into GitHub's rate limit. Right now that shows up as a generic HTTP error rather than a message that clearly says "rate limited," so if an install fails for no obvious reason, that's worth checking.

## Lock and lockfile

This is inspired by `uv.lock` and `Cargo.lock`. As long as the dependencies are declared on `baler.toml`, the command you'll use, `baler lock`, will resolve everything a project depends on, both R packages and other modules, and writes the result to `baler.lock` so future installs use the exact same versions instead of re-resolving from scratch. This doesn't install anything itself, it just pins what *would* be installed. Here's the anatomy of `baler lock` command: 

``` bash
baler lock [<path>] [--update [<pkg>...]] [--with-rver] [--check] [--remove]
```

`baler lock` is idempotent. If `baler.lock` already matches `baler.toml`, nothing is written, so running it twice, or on another machine, never shows up in a diff. If `baler.toml` changed, every pin that still fits is kept, and only what changed is added, dropped or re-resolved.

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<path>` | The project's root directory. Defaults to `.`. |
| `--update` | Ignore the existing pins and re-resolve every dependency from scratch. Use this when you want to pick up newer versions. |
| `--update <pkg>...` | Re-resolve only the named packages (e.g. `--update purrr cli`) and keep every other pin. A name that isn't in the lock is an error. |
| `--with-rver` | Also record the R version you currently have on your system inside `baler.lock`. This is informational only, it's never enforced or checked against on install. Only allowed when the lock is being created, or together with `--update`. |
| `--check` | Never write anything. Exit with an error if `baler.lock` is missing or doesn't match `baler.toml`. Meant for CI. Can't be combined with `--update`, `--with-rver` or `--remove`. |
| `--remove` | Delete `baler.lock` instead of writing one. Safe to run any time, if there's no lockfile, `{baler}` just resolves dependencies fresh each time, same as a project that never had one. |

::: callout-note
The positional form isn't a fourth way to point at something — it always collapses to one of the three rows above (a sniffed local path, `gh:user/repo`, or a bare name for `--repo`). Note that `gh:user/repo` can't take `--branch`, `--tag`, `--rev`, or `--module-dir`; those need the explicit `--git <url>` flag instead.

:::

## Uninstall a module

The bundle part gives you an archive, under `.tar.gz` format, of `{box}`-`{baler}` module. Then we have the "installation" part that archives the module and placed on the path where `~/.baler/modules` lived. `{baler}` also has an option to uninstall a previously installed module, through `baler remove`. Here's the following anatomy: 

``` bash
baler remove <name> [--force]
```

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<name>` | The name of an installed module to remove. |
| `--force` | Skip the `[y/N]` confirmation prompt and remove it immediately. |

Fails if no module with that name is currently installed, there's nothing to accidentally remove twice.
